landing.description: Track your transition in a journal with custom scales, Voice benchmarks and care records. Encrypted on your device, with no account.

privacy.description: How engender encrypts your journal, how access and recovery keys work, what exports reveal, and what the web host sees.

hero.headline: A transition tracker with a journal at its heart.

definition.sense: to cause or give rise to a feeling, situation or condition.

hero.subheadline: Track your days with custom scales, Voice benchmarks and care records. Your journal stays on your device. No account needed.

overview: engender is a transition tracker built around a journal. An entry holds a mood, a note, your scales, tags, photos, a voice recording and how your body felt. One of those is enough. Write several entries in a day or backdate one to a day you missed.

You choose which parts of transition to record. Name your own scales, compare Voice benchmarks with earlier takes, or keep medication and appointment records beside your entries. The roadmap lists steps in Poland, with room for your own goals. The app does not assess your voice or give treatment advice.
One trans person wrote this for other trans people. It is free software, there is no price, no plan and nothing to upsell, and it stays that way.
sectionPrivacy: What it protects, and what it doesn't
privacyHandoff: Your journal is encrypted on your device. There is no engender account or server holding your entries. The web host sees requests to load and update the app, but does not receive your journal.
What that protects, and what it does not, is on its own page.
tourIntro: Every screenshot here was made with invented data. Nobody's journal appears on this site.

tour.caption: The greeting, what is coming up, and the last seven days in whatever colour you picked. The mood row logs an entry for right now in one action, so on a day when you cannot face writing, you can still log something. Invented entries.
Mood, your scales, tags, a note, photos. An entry needs only one of them, so a day where all you managed was a mood is still a day you logged. Invented entry.
Coloured by mood, or by any scale you choose. Days you did not log stay neutral, because a gap is not a bad day and the colour never says it was.
Gender can shift through a day, so a day holds as many entries as it needs and stamps each one with its time. The day's own colour is their average. Invented entries.
Searches your notes and your tags as you type. Diacritics do not matter in either direction: type lozko and it finds łóżko. Invented entries.
Every scale gets its own chart and its own average over however many days you pick. Days with more than one entry are averaged, and the list behind the chart says which days those were.
Dated days that matter, in order. The ones ahead count down. The ones behind come back each year.
Export packs everything into one Archive, encrypted with a password you choose, before it goes anywhere. Invented journal.

paragraphs.rest: A mood on five levels, a note, tags, photos, a voice recording, and your scales. Several a day, or backdated to a day you missed.

Five come built in, among them Gender feeling, which runs from dysphoria at one end to euphoria at the other. Make your own, with whatever two end labels and range you want, and group the ones you use into a preset so the entry screen only asks about what you actually track.
Dysphoria and euphoria, marked on the body regions they belong to. Tracked separately, because they are not opposites and one day can hold both.
Grouped and editable. Turn a whole group off when it stops being relevant. Hiding a built-in tag takes it out of every picker and leaves every entry that already carries it alone.
Kept in the app's own storage. They never go into your phone's gallery, so they do not turn up in a camera roll someone else is scrolling.
A heat map in one colour, driven by mood or by a scale you pick.
Your notes and tag labels, matched as you type, ignoring diacritics. Star what matters, and every starred entry and photo waits in one place.
One per scale, over 7 to 365 days, with your streak. Open one for the dated list of values behind it, so you can check the line instead of taking it on trust.

For a given scale, how days with a tag compare to days without it. An observation, not a verdict. Tags with fewer than three entries in that stretch are left out, because at that size the difference is noise.
A week, a month or a year, looked back on: entries, streaks, how a scale moved, top tags, milestones, photos. Or any stretch you pick yourself.
What you logged a month, six months and a year ago. Only days that were good come back.
Two stretches of time, side by side.
One tap when you were misgendered, one when you were gendered right, and a chart of how the counts move.
Countdowns ahead, anniversaries behind.

paragraphs: The Transition tab groups the tools around your journal into Health, Steps, Support and Media.

paragraphs.rest: Measurements and clothing sizes, medication schedules and doses, lab results and modelled hormone curves. Keep records of changes, cycle events and surgery recovery. Prepare questions for appointments and print a summary for a clinician when you choose. The app does not interpret lab values or suggest doses.

Milestones, tryouts, binder and tucking wear time, hair removal and letters that open on a date you choose. The roadmap covers Poland, with social, legal, appearance and medical tracks. Add your own goals or mark a step as not for you.

On the Voice screen in Steps, record the same passage and held vowel each time, then compare with your own earlier takes. Figures such as pitch, resonance and speaking rate describe the recordings without grading your voice. A benchmark belongs to a day; a voice recording in an entry is a separate memo.
Safe Space brings back starred and positive entries and holds your own list of things that help. Trans organisations and helplines are listed in the app, so you can read the directory offline.

Browse photos from across the journal and compare two with a slider. Make a collage or time-lapse to export. Keep documents such as referrals and court orders, linked to the goal or record they belong to.
Export packs your journal into one file, encrypted with a password you choose, before it leaves the app. Import puts it back, either merged into what is here or replacing it.
On Android, an encrypted Archive written to a folder you pick, weekly or monthly.
Import a Daylio CSV. It shows you the counts and how the moods will map before it writes anything, and it only ever merges.
CSV or JSON, for a spreadsheet or for keeping your own copy. It is not encrypted, and the app says so and makes you confirm before it writes the file.

paragraphs.lead: When it has been a while.
paragraphs.rest: If your last Archive is more than 30 days old, the home screen says so once. You can dismiss it.
The same journal features as a phone app. Its data does not sync with the browser journal.
Medication, injections, appointments. One-off or repeating, as notifications on your phone.
One prompt a day, at a time you choose, skipped on days you have already written something.
Add it to your home screen and open it without a browser in the way.
Once it is installed it does not need the network to open.

features.group: If you need to be careful
paragraphs: Choose how to unlock the journal in Privacy and data. Disguise, lock on leave and quick exit are optional.

paragraphs.rest: Use a passphrase, a PIN with a device key, supported biometrics or a device-bound key. The Privacy page explains what each protects and how recovery works.
The browser tab says Notes instead of engender. On Android, the app takes a neutral name and icon too.
The journal locks when you switch away. With a mode that asks for a secret, you need it to return.
A two-finger swipe down covers the journal. Disguise shows a Notes screen; otherwise the tab goes blank. If your access mode asks for a secret, returning requires it.
, including trans, nonbinary, genderfluid, bisexual, lesbian, pansexual, agender and rainbow. Each one recolours the whole app, charts and calendar included, and each one works in light and dark.
No red for a bad day and no green for a good one. The heat map is one colour at different strengths, and an empty day stays empty.
English and Polish, switchable in settings, with dates following whichever you pick.

acquisitionIntro: engender runs in a browser. It opens straight away, with nothing to install and no account to make.
acquisitionAndroid: The Android app is the same journal as an app. These are the four places to get it, and each becomes a link as it goes live. Google Play is last for a reason.

channels.name: Aurora
channels.note: The same build as Google Play, without your Google account attached to the download.

channels.name: F-Droid
channels.note: Builds the app from source itself, so you are not trusting a file that came from me.

channels.name: Obtainium
channels.note: Follows this project's releases on GitHub and keeps itself up to date.

channels.name: Google Play
channels.note: Works, and tells Google you have a trans app on your phone. Nothing in engender changes that.

support.rest: engender is free software under the GPLv3. Do not take my word for anything on this page: the source is public. Go and look, or get someone you trust to look.

support: The licence also means you can run it, change it and pass it on. This is one person's project, so it might stop. If it does, someone else is free to pick the code up, and your Archives are a documented format rather than something only this app can open.

support.rest: , tell me what happened and what you expected instead. That is usually enough to find it.

support.lead: Do not send me your journal.
support.rest: Not an Archive, not a screenshot with your entries in it, not a log from a session where you were writing. I will never ask for any of it. If something asks, it is not me.

privacyPage.title: What engender protects, and what it does not
privacyPage.intro: Your journal is encrypted on your device. How you unlock it, where you keep backups and who can use your device determine what that protects.
privacyPage.guideLink: Read the Privacy chapter in the Guide.

sections.heading: Where your journal is
paragraphs: Your journal stays on the device where you write it. There is no engender account or server holding a copy, and no background sync. The browser and Android app hold separate journals. You can move a copy yourself with an encrypted Archive.
The app does not send your entries to the web host. Loading and updating the web app still make network requests, described below.

sections.heading: Unlocking your journal
paragraphs: A random data key encrypts the journal. Your access mode protects that key, so changing the passphrase does not require encrypting years of entries again.

paragraphs.rest: On the web or Android, a passphrase you type opens the data key through Argon2id. Save it in a password manager. I cannot recover a forgotten passphrase.

Four digits combine with a key tied to your device to protect the data key. A copied journal file alone is not enough to guess the PIN. On the web, a copy of the whole browser profile can expose the device secret. On Android, someone who can run their own code on the phone can ask Keystore for it. With that secret, there are only 10,000 PINs to try. Choose a passphrase if this is your concern.

Supported browsers can ask for your fingerprint or face before opening the journal. Web device-bound mode opens without a prompt and keeps its key in that browser profile. On Android, device-bound mode uses Keystore and the phone’s screen lock or biometrics. Android also offers a separate mode without an unlock prompt. Losing the device or browser profile can mean losing that copy of the journal.

paragraphs: Wrong PIN attempts in the app wait longer before another try. The app does not automatically erase your journal after failed attempts. This delay does not protect against guesses made outside the app.

paragraphs.rest: The journal database, its working files and the copy made before an upgrade are encrypted. Photos and thumbnails are encrypted separately under the same data key. Voice recordings use encrypted file storage too. Imports pass through memory rather than a temporary file.

The wrapped key and settings needed to open it stay outside the encrypted journal. So do theme, palette and language, disguise and lock-on-leave preferences, and timestamps of failed PIN attempts. These contain no journal entries.

sections.heading: If you lose access
paragraphs: You can create an optional recovery key and save it off the device. The app shows it once. Anyone with that key and your local journal can open the journal without your usual passphrase, PIN or biometric check.

The recovery key opens only a copy whose data still exists on that device and, on the web, in that browser profile. It does not bring back a lost device, move the journal or open an Archive. I cannot recover this key or your Archive password.
Without a working access method or a saved recovery key, resetting the app erases the local journal. A saved Archive can restore the data it contains if you still know its password.

sections.heading: Archives and readable exports
paragraphs: An Archive is a copy of your journal encrypted with a password you choose before saving or sharing the file. That password protects the Archive separately from the journal on your device. Scheduled backups on Android create encrypted Archives too.

paragraphs.rest: Its header is readable: the first six bytes spell GDIARY, followed by format and key-derivation settings. The header identifies the file as an engender Archive without revealing entries. A storage provider may also see the filename, size and access history.

paragraphs.lead: If you lose an Archive password,
paragraphs.rest: that file stays unreadable. Other Archives with different passwords are unaffected.

paragraphs: CSV and JSON exports, printable journals and clinician summaries, shared photos and other readable exports are not encrypted. Anyone who gets a file can read it. The app asks for confirmation or an explicit action before creating it. You choose where it goes.

sections.heading: What the web host can see
paragraphs: When the web app loads or checks for updates, the host sees your IP address, request time, requested files and their sizes, and User-Agent and Referer headers. It does not receive journal entries, photos, notes or lab results. After installation, you can use the journal offline.

The Android app does not request the INTERNET permission. Store operators may record downloads and updates. Installing from Google Play ties the installation to your Google account; no engender setting changes that.

sections.heading: What none of this protects against
paragraphs: Encryption at rest does not protect an open journal on your screen, data read from memory or a compromised operating system. Someone who controls your device may be able to read what you open. Readable exports also need protection wherever you save or share them.

getting-started.title: Getting started
getting-started.description: Installing engender, what onboarding asks, and why there's no account.

sections.heading: Installing
paragraphs: engender runs in a browser. Open it and you can start writing straight away, with nothing to download.

To keep it on your phone or computer, use your browser's option to install it or add it to your home screen. It then opens in its own window, and once it is installed it opens without a network connection.
There is also an Android app. It is the same journal, installed as an app, and the home page lists where you will be able to get it.

Your journal lives where you start it. A journal in your phone's browser and one in the Android app are two separate journals, and so are two browsers. To move yours from one to the other, export a backup and choose "I already have a backup" when you open the other one for the first time.

sections.heading: No account
paragraphs: There is no sign-up and no engender account. Nothing you write goes to a server: it is stored on your device, encrypted, and it leaves only when you export it yourself.
So nobody can hand your journal back if the device is lost or reset. A backup you exported is the only copy that survives, so export one every so often and keep it somewhere safe.

sections.heading: Setup
paragraphs: The first time you open engender, it asks a few questions before you reach your journal. There are nine steps, and you can change every answer later.

paragraphs.rest: What the app is. If you have a backup from before, restore it from here instead of starting a new journal.
What the app should call you. It is only used to greet you.
Pick a flag. Its colours run through the whole app.
Which gender scales you want to rate when you write an entry.
Which parts of the app are pinned to Today, your front page. Everything else is still there, one tap further in.

What opens your journal, such as a passphrase, a PIN or the fingerprint your phone already asks for. Each option says what it protects before you choose it. Nobody can recover a forgotten passphrase or PIN.
What the app may ask your phone for, such as notifications, each with a reason. You do not need any of it to write an entry.
Whether the app shows a different name and icon outside itself. It is off unless you turn it on.
Setup ends and opens Today.

paragraphs: Every step before the last has a way straight into the app, which keeps what you have chosen so far. Most steps also have a Skip, which leaves that setting as it is.

images.alt: Welcome step explains the local journal and offers setup or backup restore.
Name step asks what the app should call you and says the answer can be skipped.

home.title: Today
home.description: The first tab: what is running, what is coming up, the mood pick, pinned rows and quick add.

sections.heading: What Today shows
paragraphs: Today is the first tab, and the app opens on it. It is about what is going on now and what is next.

paragraphs.rest: Things running right now, such as a wear timer or a dose that is due. A tile shows up when there is something to say and goes once it is dealt with.

Dated things in the next thirty days: appointments, surgery dates, milestones, letters due to open and doses on a schedule that is not daily. It shows three and folds the rest, and it is not there at all when nothing is coming.
Short reminders you can dismiss, such as an old backup or a medication running low.
Five moods, from awful to great. Picking one starts today's entry.
The parts of the app you keep on Today. Each row says what is next when there is something, and when you last logged it otherwise.

paragraphs: A new journal also has a Getting started section, with a few things worth setting up early. You can ignore them and just write.

images.alt: Today shows a binder timer, upcoming appointment and milestone, and the mood question.

sections.heading: Arranging Today
paragraphs: Tap Arrange these rows to choose what is pinned and in what order, which kinds of date Coming up shows, and which live tiles can appear. The first set of pins comes from the areas you picked during setup. After that, the app never pins or moves anything by itself.

sections.heading: Quick add
paragraphs: The button in the middle of the bottom bar is quick add. It works from any screen and opens a fan of options: the five moods, an entry for an earlier day, the two tally counters, a dose, and starting or stopping a wear session. Screens that log something keep their own add button as well.

sections.heading: Where an entry goes
paragraphs: An entry started from Today, from quick add or from Journal is the same kind of entry. Journal shows it on its day, and Look back counts it with the rest.

calendar.title: Journal
calendar.description: The month heat map, single days, search, starred entries and writing an entry.

sections.heading: The month
paragraphs: Journal is the second tab, and it holds your own days. It opens on the month as a heat map. Days with entries are filled in, coloured by your mood or, if you switch it, by one of your gender scales, and a deeper colour means a higher value. No colour means good or bad.
Under the month are your recent entries, and the button below them shows five more days at a time.

images.alt: Journal month view shows a mood heat map above recent entries.

sections.heading: One day
paragraphs: Tap a day to see everything logged on it. A day can hold as many entries as you like. A day still ahead with a small mark has something planned, such as a dose or an appointment, and tapping it shows what.

images.alt: Day view shows one journal entry and planned doses beneath it.

sections.heading: Search
paragraphs: The search icon at the top of Journal opens search. Before you type, it offers your most-used tags and recent searches. Filters narrow the results by tag, mood, dates, or starred.
Star an entry you want to find again, then filter by Starred to see all of them.
You can save a search as a question. Opening it later searches your journal as it is then, not as it was when you saved it.

sections.heading: Writing an entry
paragraphs: An entry is one moment. It needs just one thing, such as a mood, a note or a photo.

The note comes first, under the date. The moods and the star sit on the save bar at the bottom. Under the note, a row of chips opens the rest one at a time: mode, gender scales, tags, the body map, and attachments such as photos and voice recordings.
The body map is where you mark how a part of your body feels. Pick a spot, then slide towards dysphoria or towards euphoria. Leaving it in the middle records nothing.

stats.title: Look back
stats.description: Choosing a stretch of time, the readings, Wrapped, On this day and the tally.

sections.heading: Choosing a stretch
paragraphs: Look back is the third tab. Everything on it reads one stretch of time, which you choose on the timeline at the top: drag its two ends, or pick a stretch from the list. The timeline also shows your eras, milestones, regimen, tryouts and surgeries, and tapping one picks its dates.
Just under the timeline are the plain facts for that stretch: how many entries, the average on a scale, and which scale moved the furthest.

images.alt: Look back shows a selected date range, entry count and reading summary.

sections.heading: Readings
paragraphs: Below that is a grid of readings. Each tile shows one figure for the stretch, and tapping it opens the full reading. A tile with nothing to show for the stretch is left out.

paragraphs.rest: One scale or your mood across the stretch, day after day.
Each day as a point on two scales, which you can play through in order.
How many days landed at each mood, and what you wrote about.
Words that turn up more often in this stretch than in the rest of your journal.

paragraphs.lead: Tags, and how a scale moved.
paragraphs.rest: Which tags came with a scale going up or down.
Your highest days on a scale you choose, each one a tap from its entries.
How each part of the body has felt over the stretch, towards dysphoria or towards euphoria.
Two periods side by side. It starts with your stretch against the same length of time just before it.
The tags your good and starred entries carry most.

sections.heading: Wrapped and On this day
paragraphs: Two more tiles sit under the grid. You can turn either one off in Settings.

paragraphs.rest: A look back at a finished week, month or year, or at the stretch you picked: entries, mood, the scale that moved furthest, tags, milestones and photos. You can share it as a card, and the card never carries your writing or your photos.
A good day from a month, six months or a year ago, with any letter written or opened on it. Days that went badly are not brought back.

sections.heading: Tally
paragraphs: Tally counts how often you were misgendered and how often people got it right, and shows both over time. Quick add adds to either count from anywhere.

health.title: Health
health.description: Care and your medication, measurements and sizes, the surgery journey, appointments and the clinician summary.

sections.heading: The Transition tab
paragraphs: The fourth tab, Transition, has four groups: Health, Steps, Support and Media. Search at the top finds group rows by name and searches text in your journal.
Health is the first group.

sections.heading: Care
paragraphs: Care is where your medication lives. Each drug in a running regimen gets its own lane. The timeline marks your latest lab draw. For each regimen, Care shows the dose and route, your last dose, when the next one is expected and how much you have left, with the projected run-out day.
Four screens open from Care:

paragraphs.rest: What you take, how and how often, from the day you started. You can pause it or end it, and it stays in your history. If you switch it on, a schedule records an expected dose as taken after that day ends. You can correct it or mark it skipped.
Every dose taken, skipped or changed, at the time it happened.
Your results, as you entered them. Results in different units stay on separate lines.
A drawing of how your doses rise and fall over time. It is not a prediction of your levels. Your own lab results can calibrate it.

paragraphs: Stock is a count you enter now and then. Logged doses feed the stock estimate and projected run-out day, as well as supported hormone curves. Care warns when stock is running low. It also shows the running window's medication-days total; the full exposure history is in the clinician visit summary.

images.alt: Care shows medication lanes with lab draw, last dose, next dose and stock dates.

sections.heading: Changes you've noticed
paragraphs: Under the medication, Care keeps the changes you've noticed. Pick a change from the list or add your own, and mark the day you first noticed it. Side effects go here too, each with how strong it was, from 1 to 5. The more private categories, such as genital and sexual changes, start switched off.

paragraphs.rest: Your hair on a published scale, Norwood-Hamilton or Sinclair, or in your own words, with photos taken from the same spot.
A period, spotting, or nothing this month. They only show while a testosterone regimen is running, or once you turn on Cycle tracking in Settings.

images.alt: Changes you have noticed shows a dated timeline of effects recorded in the journal.

sections.heading: Measurements and sizes
paragraphs: Waist, hips, chest and underbust are built in, and you can add any measurement you like. Weight and height are not built in, so add them yourself if you want them. Measuring consistently, beside the chart, says how to measure the same way each time.
Sizes are what you bought and how it fit: the kind of garment, the size, the brand and a note. Nothing is converted between brands.

sections.heading: Surgery journey
paragraphs: Each surgery gets its own journey, named however you like. It holds the consults before it, the date once you have one, and afterwards a day count, photos, notes and your own checklist.
If your surgeon gave you a dilation schedule, type it in and log your sessions against it.

sections.heading: Appointments
paragraphs: Appointments opens on your next visit and how far away it is. Under it is What to raise, your list of things to bring up, which carries over from one visit to the next.
At the visit, In the room goes through your questions one at a time, with space for what they said. Past visits are under Behind you, and the app asks how each one went.
The clinician visit summary is a page to print for a doctor: doses, lab results and side effects for dates you choose. You see it exactly as it will print. Open it from Care or from Appointments.

sections.heading: What Health does not do
paragraphs: Nothing in Health says whether a number is good or bad, suggests a dose or tells you what to do. It keeps what you enter and draws it.

steps.title: Steps
steps.description: Milestones and eras, tryouts, voice, wear time, hair removal, the roadmap and time-capsule letters.

sections.heading: Milestones and eras
paragraphs: Steps is the second group on the Transition tab.

A milestone is a day that mattered, or will. One still ahead counts down, and one behind you comes back each year as an anniversary. You can note how it felt when you add it and again on each anniversary.
Eras are stretches of time you name yourself, such as "before I knew". They show as bands behind your milestones, and Look back can use one as its stretch. You make and edit them in Settings.

sections.heading: Tryouts
paragraphs: A tryout is something you are trying: a name or pronouns, a style, a garment, makeup, or a step in how you present. It has a start date and, once you stop, an end date. Note how it feels as often as you like, and add photos. Several can run at once.

sections.heading: Voice
paragraphs: Practice, the voice benchmark and your recordings share one screen.

A benchmark is a take made the same way every time: the same passage read and the same vowel held. That keeps takes months apart comparable. It shows figures such as pitch and speaking rate next to your own earlier takes, and gives no verdict on your voice.

sections.heading: Wear time
paragraphs: Wear time is for binder, tucking and compression wear. Start a timer, or fill in a session afterwards, with a note on comfort or pain. You can set a reminder for a number of hours you choose. With a binder, a quiet cue appears at eight hours, and you can turn it off.
The screen also shows binder safety guidance and its sources.

sections.heading: Hair removal
paragraphs: Hair removal logs electrolysis and laser sessions, with the area, method, pain, cost, provider and photos. The screen shows how long it has been since the last one.

sections.heading: The roadmap
paragraphs: The transition roadmap lists the steps of the Polish transition procedure. Poland is the only country so far. The steps are roadmap goals, grouped into four roadmap tracks: social, legal, presentation and medical.
Goals can be done in any order, and no track waits on another. Tick a goal once it is done, or mark it not my path. You can mark a whole track the same way, and put it back later.
You can add your own goals to any track, and file documents against a goal.
The roadmap describes the procedure and never says what to do in your own case. It shows the date its content was last checked against its sources.

images.alt: Transition roadmap shows the Polish pack and checklist goals in the social track.

sections.heading: Time-capsule letters
paragraphs: Write a letter to yourself and pick the day it opens. It stays sealed until then, and after that you can read it whenever you like. Letters about to open show on Today, under Coming up.
The Open section also shows the photos you have starred.

support.title: Support
support.description: Safe space for the hard days, and the directory of trans organisations and helplines.

sections.heading: Safe space
paragraphs: Support is the third group on the Transition tab.
Safe space is for the moments when dysphoria is too much. It opens on box breathing. Below that are four things:

paragraphs.rest: Past entries you tagged as good, or starred.
Your own list: who to text, which walk, which song. It starts empty.
The directory described below.
A link to the Look back reading of the tags your good entries carry most.

paragraphs: Opening Safe space writes nothing to your journal.

images.alt: Good moments in Safe space lists starred and tagged journal entries.

sections.heading: Support and resources
paragraphs: Support and resources lists trans organisations and helplines, each with a line on what it offers and a number or an address. It comes with the app, so you can read it with no signal. The list does not include general emergency or crisis numbers.
The screen says when every entry was last checked. Tapping a number or an address hands it to your phone or browser, which leaves the app.

images.alt: Support and resources lists contacts with Poland and English-language filters.

media.title: Media
media.description: Every photo in your journal in one library, and the documents you keep.

sections.heading: Photos
paragraphs: Media is the fourth group on the Transition tab.
Photos is every photo in your journal in one dated list: from entries, milestones, hair progress, hair removal, tryouts and surgery. The chips at the top narrow it down by where a photo came from.

Pick two photos and drag the divider across them to compare the earlier one with the later. For an export, choose a date range and make a collage or timelapse from selected photos. You can preview it before sharing.
Photos stay inside the app and never go to your phone's gallery. To change or delete one, open the entry or record it belongs to.

images.alt: Progress photos shows source filters and a grid of dated photos.

sections.heading: Documents
paragraphs: Documents holds the papers you keep, such as opinions, diagnoses, referrals, court rulings and invoices. Each has a date, a title you write and the file itself. You can link a document to a roadmap goal, a milestone, a surgery journey or a regimen.
The index groups documents by what each paper proves. Photos and PDFs have thumbnails. The app never reads what a document says, so you find one by its title.

settings.title: Settings
settings.description: What's a preference in engender, and what lives elsewhere instead.

sections.heading: What belongs here
paragraphs: Settings holds preferences and the lists those preferences draw from. You choose how the journal looks and what it asks you to track here. You make entries and read their history on the screens those records belong to.

For example, Settings holds a reminder's schedule. The words and details you want to remember stay with the entry or feature the reminder is about. Doses, labs and surgery notes live in Health, not in Settings.

images.alt: Settings shows flag palettes, mood colours and theme controls under Appearance.

sections.heading: Appearance
paragraphs: Appearance lets you choose the app's language, theme, gender palette and mood colours. The palette has eight choices; mood colours have their own presets. You can also adjust text size, legibility and motion.

sections.heading: Tracking
paragraphs: Tracking holds your active gender scales and the reference lists used across the journal: dimensions, body regions, affirmations, tag groups, modes, entry templates and eras. You can also set a journaling pause and choose words that Look back skips when it finds words that stand out.
Reminders set when you want a nudge. Notifications gives the app's other prompts one place to switch them on or off. Live tiles are switched in Today's editor, beside its pins and agenda kinds.

Live tiles and phone notifications share one list of kinds, even though their switches sit on different screens. A live tile appears when your journal gives it something to show. Phone notifications can arrive when you scheduled one or when an export fails. Look back offers can notify you too if you switch them on. Quiet hours hold notifications until the window ends; they do not erase them.

sections.heading: Privacy and data
paragraphs: Privacy and data holds security and access choices, permissions and the disguise switch. Export is where you make or restore a backup and import from Daylio. Journal book prints a chosen range. Trash keeps deleted entries for 30 days before they are removed.

privacy.title: Privacy
privacy.description: Where journal data lives, how it is encrypted, and what happens when you export or share it.

sections.heading: Where the journal lives
paragraphs: The journal stays in storage on the device where you use it. There is no account, profile on a server, analytics or journal upload. A browser and the Android app keep separate journals; so do two browser profiles.

When the web app loads or updates, its host can see your IP address, the time of the request, which files the browser asks for and their sizes, plus the User-Agent and referrer headers. That is app traffic. Entries, photos, notes and lab results are not sent to the host. The web app does make network requests to load and update; the journal data stays on your device.

sections.heading: Encryption and access
paragraphs: The database is encrypted as a database, including its side files and the copy made before an upgrade changes it. Photos and thumbnails sit outside it, so each file is encrypted separately with the same random data key. Imports run through memory and never touch a temporary file. Sensitive boot data is encrypted too. The app does not claim that every file on the device is encrypted: the wrapped key and the settings needed to open it, your theme, palette and language, lock-on-leave and disguise choices, and the PIN attempt timestamps remain outside. None of those items is journal content.

The data key is random. On the web, your Journal passphrase is processed with Argon2id and used to wrap that key with AES-GCM. The database uses the data key itself, not your passphrase. This lets you change the passphrase without encrypting the journal again. The usable key stays in memory; after the browser session ends, you need the passphrase again. You can also open the web journal with a four-digit PIN and a device-bound key, biometric verification through WebAuthn PRF on a supported browser, or a device-bound key that needs no in-app prompt. That last key stays in its browser profile; clearing site storage, resetting the profile or losing the device can make the local copy unreadable.

Android has four access modes: a device-bound key gated by the phone's screen lock or biometric check; an unlocked mode using SQLCipher and a Keystore key, with no in-app prompt; a four-digit PIN with a hardware-backed key; or a typed passphrase processed with Argon2id. Android Keystore releases its key only after the phone checks who is asking.

A recovery key is optional. It has 25 characters and is shown once; the app does not store it off the device. It can open a web journal only on the device and browser profile that still hold the journal. On Android, it can open the journal on that device if your credentials fail. It cannot move the journal or decrypt an Archive. Without a recovery key, lost credentials cannot be recovered by the maintainer. A forgotten Archive password cannot be recovered either.

images.alt: Settings' Disguise and quick exit panel shows disguise and lock-on-leave switches.

sections.heading: Android and network access
paragraphs: The Android app does not request the INTERNET permission. In normal use it opens no network sockets and sends no journal data to a server. Store operators may still record installs and updates under their own policies once Android releases are available.

Android asks for POST_NOTIFICATIONS, SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM and RECEIVE_BOOT_COMPLETED to deliver reminders and the daily check-in, use the time you chose, and restore them after a restart. It asks for RECORD_AUDIO and MODIFY_AUDIO_SETTINGS for voice notes, and CAMERA for video notes. A still photo opens the phone's camera app instead. Notifications show a generic label by default, including on a locked screen; you can choose to show the title. Android removes a copied recovery key from the clipboard after one minute.

sections.heading: Archives and other exports
paragraphs: You choose where an exported or shared file goes. A cloud drive or document provider can see its filename, timestamp and size, along with account access records.

An encrypted .ttbackup Archive, exported by you or scheduled on Android, uses chunked AES-256-GCM and a password you choose. The password protects that Archive, not the journal on your device. Its header stays readable: the first six bytes say GDIARY, followed by the format version, Argon2id settings and salt. The app needs that information to recognise the file and derive its key. The header reveals the format, not your entries. Anyone without the password cannot read the Archive.

Some exports are deliberately readable: CSV and JSON data, journal books for printing or PDF, clinician summaries, photo collages and timelapses, shared Wrapped cards, saved PDFs, and single-event .ics calendar files. Anyone who receives one can read what it contains. The app asks you to confirm or take an explicit action before it makes an unencrypted file.

images.alt: Export and import shows backup age and the encrypted export form.

sections.heading: Security reports
paragraphs: You can report a security problem through GitHub's private vulnerability reporting. Include the app version, device or browser, clear steps to reproduce the problem, and what you expected and saw. Use invented data for a minimal proof. Do not send journal entries, Archives, keys, screenshots with private details or logs containing journal content. Nobody needs to see your journal for support or to confirm a bug.
One person maintains the project, so a report is read when they next sit down to work. There is no fixed response window.

contributing.title: Contributing
contributing.description: Code, country packs and translations - three ways to help.

sections.heading: Code
paragraphs: Clone the Journal repository from github.com/barankiewicz/gender-diary. Run npm install, then npm run dev to work locally. The README lists the checks; npm run check, npm test and npm run test:browser cover different parts of the app.

Keep a pull request focused. Say what changed, why it changed and which checks you ran. CI runs on each pull request, including browser checks. Use invented journal data in tests and screenshots; do not put anyone's real journal in an issue or a pull request.

sections.heading: Country packs
paragraphs: You don't need to write code to help with a country pack. A pack is bundled into the app and describes one country's transition procedure as roadmap goals. Each goal sits in one of four roadmap tracks: social, legal, presentational or medical. Only the Polish pack ships today.

Cite sources for each goal you propose and record when you checked them; the pack's reviewedOn date is shown in the app because procedures change. Describe what a step involves, never what someone should do in their own case. You can send sourced corrections or draft goals without editing the app.

sections.heading: Translations
paragraphs: The Journal keeps screen text in messages/en.json and messages/pl.json. Adding a language means adding its message catalogue and checking each screen with the real text, including long labels and small phones.

Read docs/ui-copy.md in the Journal repository before writing. It sets the voice for labels, explanations and risk screens. Translate the meaning, then edit for natural wording in the new language. The app supports English and Polish today; another language needs its own complete pass.
